Finland's coast guard stated it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials noted.

Sources indicate that "War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.".

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry noted a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

While Besprozvannykh initially remarked the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.

Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, mentioned during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.

The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Finnish Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry mentioned.

Sources indicate that the Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

Breaking: How to pair your Bluetooth headphones to your Windows PC

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (456 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bluetooth headphones and earbuds are now incredibly common, and more people than ever own a pair.
  • On paper, connecting headphones to a Windows 11 computer is relatively straightforward.
  • Then, put your device in pairing mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bluetooth headphones and earbuds are now incredibly common, and more people than ever own a pair. But despite how long Bluetooth has been around, pairing Bluetooth headphones to a computer can still be fiddly. Microsoft hasn't helped, either, with Windows 11's Bluetooth stability a constant bugbear, too, making things even worse — but more on that later.

On paper, connecting headphones to a Windows 11 computer is relatively straightforward. The simplest way is to click the speaker icon in the bottom-right of the taskbar to open the quick settings panel, click the arrow next to the Bluetooth icon, and make sure the Bluetooth toggle is set to the on position.

Then, put your device in pairing mode. How you enter pairing mode differs between products, so refer to the documentation for your specific headphones or earbuds. You'll usually need to hold down a button, often with the Bluetooth logo. Select your device when it appears in the list of Bluetooth devices, and you're connected.

In a recent development, connecting your Bluetooth earbuds or headphones to a Windows 11 PC is simple when things work correctly, but that doesn't always happen. Bluetooth performance has long been a weak point on Windows 11, and Microsoft was still trying to improve things as of September 2026. If things don't work, you're probably not doing anything wrong and should look into other solutions, like updating your wireless drivers or rebooting your PC.

It has been revealed that you can also pair Bluetooth headphones by pressing Win + I to open Windows 11's Settings and selecting Bluetooth & devices from the left-hand menu. Make sure that Bluetooth is on, as indicated by the toggle. Below that toggle, you'll see the name your PC shows up as on other devices, which only matters if the device you're pairing has a screen. If you're pairing for the first time, click Add device, then click Bluetooth. Make sure your headphones are in pairing mode. The PC will begin to scan for ready-to-pair Bluetooth devices. Once your device appears in the Windows dialog, click it, and it should pair after a few moments.

Recent findings suggest that some Bluetooth accessories support Swift Pair, which tries to proactively pair devices. Popular headphones, including the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro — and previous models from those product lines — come with the feature. To set up a device with Swift Pair, make sure Bluetooth is enabled on your PC, then turn the device on and put it into pairing mode. You should see a pop-up on the PC asking if you want to connect with that device. Click Connect. Devices connected via Swift Pair will automatically connect to your PC.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting consumers’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she remarked. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”.

Recent findings suggest that signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

That mentioned, consumers can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US tech company Nvidia mentioned on Monday that it had resinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO "effective immediately.".

This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the company," Nvidia noted, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead.".

Meanwhile, the 63-year-old remarked in a statement that he was "honored" to return to the tech giant and that he would take on the renewed responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.".

He thanked interim CEO Colette Kress, who is set to return to her role as chief financial officer.

In a recent development, "I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang said. "Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work.".

US President Donald Trump rapidly commented on the development online, saying it was the "correct and proper decision" and referring to Huang by his first name as a "Great Patriot and National Treasure.".

"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote, also saying that the US had no evidence of him engaging in unlawful conduct.

According to recent reports, huang liked to flaunt his personal relationship with Trump. He was reportedly influential in convincing the US president to allow the export of higher-quality Nvidia chips to China that are useful in AI development than other US officials and entrepreneurs endorsed.

The decision was announced as trading started for the new week in New York.

The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week.

The announcement prompted a rapid early-morning rally on Wall Street, including Nvidia stocks rising back into a region between $160 and $170.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Huang quit earlier this month after admitting to extramarital affairs in a note to employees.

This concession came amid widespread reporting in the US linking him romantically to one woman in particular, who was running a major Nvidia client called Megaspeed based in Singapore and who was stated to be an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

Her company is also suspected of diverting chips not approved for export to China to the Chinese market, circumventing US sanctions.

According to recent reports, while these allegations have not been proven, they appeared to be based on the assessments of US and other western intelligency agencies, and to be information that was known for around a year. One possible indication of this was Singapore refusing the Chinese national entry into the country earlier in 2026.

Bola Tinubu promised to address the country's electricity problems while campaigning for the 2023 election.

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.

He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.

He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.

Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.

He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [thereâs punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].

Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.

Last year, 10bn naira (Â£5.5m; $7.2m), was allocated in the budget for the installation of a solar mini-grid in the Aso Villa as part of efforts to address rising electricity bills and unstable power supply.

Some reports say it has been completed and is in the testing phase, with looks to fully disconnect the facility from the national grid soon.

Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.

Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.

The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.

Many Nigerians rely on generators like these to power their homes and businesses.

Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.

According to recent reports, in 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.

"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,â he said.

Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (Â£1.5bn) investment in a new EastâWest Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.

Tinubu defeated the countryâs former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

#138764. Can a TV be too large? An investigation

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1063 w)

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Can a TV be too large? An investigation

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.
  • Sources indicate that the organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry.
  • Industry observers note that they are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.

Sources indicate that the organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows.

In short: They look way better.

Industry observers note that they are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the firm’s mid-range unit released in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that at first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic.

However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache.

Recent findings suggest that I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their significant new toy is breaking their brain.

According to recent reports, “I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor, who mentioned they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.”.

Recent findings suggest that others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too substantial and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?”.

Recent findings suggest that there doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen.

Sources indicate that finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having.

It has been revealed that in considering my nausea, one theory that sprang to mind was that it might just be my eyes’ inexperience with viewing such a significant screen. The TV was so large that it often felt like my eye had to trace different parts of the screen to take in the whole picture and, if the scene involved significant motion (most movie scenes do, after all), it conjured the sensation of trying to stare too intently at something out the window of a moving car.

After a few days, however, my eyes finally adjusted. The nausea was gone. All that remained was an immense and beautiful home viewing experience that made every previous viewing experience pale by comparison.

In a recent development, initial physiological reactions aside, the size of the 65-inch screen (and whether your living space actually has room for it) is still something that needs to be considered carefully by potential buyers. I recently moved into a place with a slightly bigger living room, which has given me the flexibility to install a bigger device. At my old apartment, however, this size of TV would have definitely felt like it was devouring the space.

It has been revealed that another slight frustration is that the C4 does not come with any detailed installation instructions. The screen (which is so wide it’s difficult to move without another person there to help you) comes detached from its base, and the user is just sort of expected to figure out how to effectively move and put together the two pieces. A quick YouTube video is all that is necessary to understand this process, but you have to be careful when moving and assembling the pieces so as not to scratch or damage the screen.

Once the whole thing is set up and assembled, the OLED is a truly beautiful thing to behold. The customization that’s possible, including advanced brightness and color control — and things like “Filmmaker Mode” (which claims to adjust each movie’s color and frame rate settings to those intended by the director) — make the user experience really powerful.

To sum up: The evo C4 is a really spectacular piece of equipment that has a lot to offer the avid home entertainment viewer — although there may be a bit of a learning curve before it makes your cinema dreams come true.

#138762. Industry News: What is Sound Glow on HomePods, and how do you get it on your Apple speaker?

Industry News: What is Sound Glow on HomePods, and how do you get it on your Apple speaker?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple’s latest HomePod update makes the top of your speaker glow in sync with music.
  • Recent findings suggest that apple's HomePod has a basic set of lights on top that don't do much beyond glowing when Siri is listening or when something is playing.
  • Sources indicate that homePods don't have a traditional display like Apple's HomeView.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s latest HomePod update makes the top of your speaker glow in sync with music.

Recent findings suggest that apple's HomePod has a basic set of lights on top that don't do much beyond glowing when Siri is listening or when something is playing. But following the launch of the HomePod mini 2, Apple also introduced a fresh feature called Sound Glow that makes better use of these lights. When turned on, the top of the speaker becomes a colorful light show synced to the song you're listening to — and the good news is that it's not exclusive to the latest HomePod mini. The feature is part of HomePod Software 27.2 and also works with the original HomePod mini and the HomePod 2 (the larger model). Here's a breakdown of how Sound Glow works and how you can enable (or disable) it on your HomePods.

Sources indicate that homePods don't have a traditional display like Apple's HomeView. Instead, Apple has included an array of LEDs on top along with a touch-sensitive surface that lets users access quick controls such as volume and play/pause. With the latest HomePod software patch, these LEDs are now used to make HomePods a little more fun with Sound Glow. Now, when you play a song, the speaker pulls colors from the album art and pulses them in time with the music's beat. Listening to Taylor Swift's The Life of a Showgirl will result in predominantly green and orange lights, while Miley Cyrus's Endless Summer Vacation will make the lights on your HomePod turn blue.

Apple indicates that the light animation reacts in real time to the bass and treble of the song being played, so two songs from the same album will glow differently. Also, Sound Glow isn't limited to songs — it also works with podcasts and Apple's ambient sounds. For instance, the Rain soundscape features an animation with a gentle pitter-patter effect. Songs without artwork or videos revert to the HomePod's standard white light. It all happens automatically and you really don't have to think about it.

There are a few limitations worth noting, though. Don't expect Sound Glow to fully light up your living room — the lights aren't bright enough to do that unless the room is completely dark. The feature is also not available on the original HomePod released in 2018, even though it can be updated to the latest HomePod software. You'll also need an Apple Intelligence-enabled device paired with your HomePods for Sound Glow to work — that means an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, an M1 Mac or newer or one of the latest iPads. An Apple TV running tvOS 27 also does the trick to enable Sound Glow on your HomePods.

If you have HomePods and a compatible Apple device, setting up Sound Glow is easy, but you'll need to make sure they're all running the latest software first. That means HomePod Software 27.2 or later on your HomePods and iOS 27.2 on your iPhone or iPad. HomePods usually enhancement automatically after a while, but you can confirm in the Home app from another Apple device. Tap the three-dot button and select Home Settings, then look for the Software Update menu. Even a brand-new HomePod mini 2 may need a software update, since it may ship with a version prior to 27.2 installed.

Once everything is up to date, you can finally enable Sound Glow. Go back to the Home app's main screen and tap your HomePod, then go to Settings and scroll down until you find the Sound Glow toggle. Just flip it on, and the feature will work — you'll need to do this for each HomePod individually. Ask Siri to play a song or use AirPlay on your iPhone to try out Sound Glow and see if it's working. And if you don't like Sound Glow, turning it off requires pretty much the same steps as turning it on, but now you'll have to flip the toggle to off instead.

Breaking: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
  • Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's FÃ©lix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right).

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.

This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.

On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was unveiled in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna GnassingbÃ© as mediator.

Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".

DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

In a recent development, DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.

DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.

When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was released in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.

DR Congo noted naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader.

Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.

Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.

He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the fresh rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.

Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other concerns including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.

The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, mentioned the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.

Tedros mentioned heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.

More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

#138758. GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (776 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them.
  • It has been revealed that the global food system is ultimately driven by demand.
  • With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our upcoming research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

It has been revealed that the global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.

Sources indicate that food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Sources indicate that lower demand from GLP-1 customers, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.

It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease,” blaming individual people for not having enough willpower. But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located, and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.

Industry observers note that the UK government-commissioned national food strategy, finalized in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.

Our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.

Industry observers note that A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables, and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use, and the environment.

According to recent reports, rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.

Industry observers note that GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.

According to recent reports, the remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with newly introduced clarity, just how closely human health, food production, and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.

Roslyn Henry is Lecturer, School of Biological Sciences, University of Aberdeen and Peter Alexander is Professor of Global Food Systems, University of Edinburgh.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, Nepal's relationship with India was shaped by familiar faces, as leaders of the Himalayan country's erstwhile three major parties took turns in the prime minister's office through revolving coalition governments.
  • This week's state visit to India by Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician, marked a clear break from that pattern.
  • As a young, first-time prime minister with a strong electoral mandate , Shah represents a new political force in Kathmandu.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, Nepal's relationship with India was shaped by familiar faces, as leaders of the Himalayan country's erstwhile three major parties took turns in the prime minister's office through revolving coalition governments.

This week's state visit to India by Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician, marked a clear break from that pattern.

As a young, first-time prime minister with a strong electoral mandate , Shah represents a new political force in Kathmandu.

But long-standing economic strain, along with August's devastating flash floods and the Nepalese public's high hopes for more jobs, investment and better governance at home, have made Shah's first bilateral visit abroad more than a mere diplomatic box-ticking exercise.

To safeguard Nepal's flood recovery and development, Shah needs to get off on the right foot with India, his country's southern neighbor and largest trading partner, and its long-standing prime minister, Narendra Modi.

While Nepal and India share an open border as well as deep cultural and historical ties, their relationship has also been marked by territorial disputes and a desire in Nepal to be seen as an equal by its much larger and more powerful neighbor.

Constantino Xavier, a senior fellow at the Center for Social and Economic Progress in New Delhi, however, cautioned against expecting too much from a single visit.

"We need a big, long-term ambition coupled with small, short-term steps," he told DW, arguing that economic cooperation should remain the central focus of relations because it directly contributes to the socioeconomic development of both countries.

The young prime minister's test is to turn a strong domestic electoral mandate and political goodwill with Latest Delhi into tangible economic gain, as well as to address longstanding border disputes and a massive trade imbalance.

Shah's administration sees diplomacy as key to addressing the country's development aspirations, which was reflected in bilateral talks with Modi on Monday.

Economic cooperation featured prominently during the talks as both sides sought engagements in trade, investment, connectivity and infrastructure development.

Kathmandu's priority was securing Indian financial support for reconstruction following the August disaster that claimed the lives of more than 1,450 people, while 5,745 are missing or unaccounted for.

The floods swept away roads, bridges, hydropower projects and settlements, with reconstruction bills estimated at around $4.8 billion (about €4.4 billion).

At a joint press briefing after their talks in Latest Delhi, Modi announced a package of $1.63 billion to help rebuild flood-hit areas and upgrade other infrastructure projects — around $380 million as a grant, with the rest as a concessional loan.

The South Asian neighbors also agreed to deepen cooperation across a wide range of areas, including trade, investment, connectivity and people-to-people ties, and debuted a upcoming long-term vision aimed at strengthening economic integration and development.

The talks also yielded commitments to broaden educational and innovation partnerships, boost energy and infrastructure cooperation, improve market access and trade links, and enhance landlocked Nepal's connectivity through additional air and port access via India.

Shah's visit offered an opportunity to break the ice in a high-level exchange visit and improve a relationship periodically strained by political mistrust, territorial disputes and differing strategic interests.

Nepal and India both have competing territorial claims over Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura, a strategic Himalayan territory in northwestern Nepal.

It has been revealed that as mayor of Kathmandu, Shah raised the border disputes with India, which helped boost his nationalist image and set his broader political agenda. However, his India visit steered clear of such contentious issues.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Foreign Minister of Nepal, said Shah avoided tricky bilateral issues to focus on his administration's economic agenda.

Sources indicate that "This visit could be a good starting point towards resolving the border challenges that have been the key strain in our relations," she told DW. "But the new government didn't show interest or the guts to address this.".

Ashok Swain, head of the Department of Peace and Conflict Research at Sweden's Uppsala University, noted the visit's success should be measured by whether the two countries can establish a predictable and mutually beneficial relationship.

"Nepal's territorial disputes, concerns over the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and its economic and transit dependence on India need to be addressed," Swain told DW.

"Shah's biggest opportunity is to transform Nepal's geographical location between India and China from a strategic vulnerability into an economic and diplomatic asset," he added, arguing that Nepal should not be forced to choose between its two neighbors.

Whether the visit marks a tangible reset on the economic front will ultimately depend not on the number of agreements announced, but on how they are implemented and whether the two governments are willing to address the disputes that have long strained ties.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oregon and Virginia remarked the company broke state consumer protection laws.

The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia have filed lawsuits against SpaceX Super Intelligence, accusing Elon Musk's conglomerate company of violating state consumer protection laws by allowing users of its Grok AI chatbot to create non-consensual sexually explicit content. The lawsuit alleged that SpaceXSI released Grok's "spicy mode" as a way to "push its lagging product to tens of millions of fresh users," which allowed for the creation of child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

In a recent development, "This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the manufacturer's false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform," Jay Jones, Virginia's attorney general, stated in a press release. "When xAI allowed Grok's creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it.".

This morning, X Safety posted that people using Grok for sexually explicit deepfakes "deliberately" violated the Terms of Service, adding that it will "keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics." X Safety also said that "protecting children is non-negotiable" and that CSAM "has no place on X or in Grok, and neither do explicit images of real people made without their consent.".

In a recent development, X Safety's post also stated that the company would "take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement," when customers circumvent Grok's safeguards to create this type of content. Earlier this year, SpaceXSI filed a lawsuit against one of its users for creating sexual images of real people without their consent.

Industry observers note that beyond Oregon and Virginia, SpaceXSI faced several regulatory investigations and lawsuits in response to people generating illegal content. The City of Baltimore pursued legal action against Musk's company, claiming that Grok broke the city's Consumer Protection Ordinance; the UK's media authority and the California attorney general released separate investigations into xAI and Grok.

Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.

It has been revealed that there are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?

According to recent reports, A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.

Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.

Sources indicate that A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.

Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.

Uber stated that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.

According to recent reports, las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he mentioned. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.).

In a recent development, that would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.

It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.

Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes.

GM has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, according to one source, who noted it’s possible that the board has other executive search firms working on this as well. The board is taking a two-track approach to its search, which is occurring simultaneously.

Industry observers note that the first is focused on traditional yet transformative automotive CEOs. One name that has come up from the executive search firm is José Muñoz, who is president and CEO of Hyundai. The board is also interested in someone less traditional. The firm has apparently floated names like Doug Field, who recently became CEO of Mind Robotics, and Larry Culp of GE, according to a source with direct information.

There are internal GM folks who are also in the mix, including Sterling Anderson, co-founder of self-driving trucks company Aurora who became chief product officer at GM in May 2025, and Paul Jacobson, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Extra forces have been deployed to guard the facility where 'Chapo Isidro' is in custody.

Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.

The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.

Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.

The ministry mentioned the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.

In a statement published on social media, external, the ministry of defence remarked that one of the detainees was under age.

It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.

The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.

It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".

Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capital.

Mexico's defence ministry stated its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.

They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.

Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued, in which four soldiers and 16 "members of organised crime" were killed, according to the latest figure released by the defence minister on Monday.

Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "SerafÃ­n", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.

As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.

There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.

US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".

"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".

The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the JuÃ¡rez cartel decades ago.

He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the BeltrÃ¡n Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.

As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.

The US Treasury mentioned at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".

It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.

According to think tank Insight Crime, external, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.

The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration stated that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".

His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

What the green flashing light on your Roku remote is telling you

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A remote that won't cooperate can put your streaming looks on hold.
  • Regardless of what you think of Fox's takeover, Roku is still an undeniable force in smart TVs.
  • According to recent reports, one of the reasons for the platform's popularity is its simplicity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A remote that won't cooperate can put your streaming looks on hold. Here's how to work out what's wrong and get back to the content you love.

Regardless of what you think of Fox's takeover, Roku is still an undeniable force in smart TVs. The company's products are an easy choice when looking for the best streaming devices, and of course a number of TVs now ship with Roku OS built in, most notably models from TCL and Hisense. Roku is the main game in town for brands that are not using Google TV, Fire TV or their own proprietary software.

According to recent reports, one of the reasons for the platform's popularity is its simplicity. That stated, there are times when the platform can be a little obtuse, mysterious blinking lights on the remote being a prime example. It's easy to assume that means a problem — but what, exactly?

If you're dealing with a flashing green LED on your Roku remote, the fix could be very straightforward, simply requiring fresh batteries or a recharge, depending on the model. In some circumstances, however, you may need to do more or replace your remote entirely. Hopefully you've already got the Roku app on your phone as a backup, which can save you in a pinch when your remote is on the fritz.

Industry observers note that as we just suggested, one reason for the light may be that your remote's batteries are low. If that's the case, swapping in new batteries (if there's no built-in one) should quickly solve the problem. If you find this is happening too frequently, though, it may be because you're using rechargeable batteries. Alkalines are costlier in the long run — but Roku does recommend them for remotes with replaceable batteries. You can check battery levels in advance by navigating to Settings > Remotes & devices > Remotes > Your remote > About.

It has been revealed that you'll also see this light if you're trying to set up a replacement remote. Using your old one or the Roku app, you may need to head to Settings > Remotes & devices > Add devices > Remote > Continue to complete the process. You'll definitely see green flashing if you trigger a remote's physical pairing controls, which is done by holding a dedicated button or the Back and Home buttons simultaneously for five seconds.

There's no need to be worried unless the light is flashing rapidly after re-pairing. If that's going on, it's a sign that your remote is probably broken and needs to be replaced. Note that you can also buy third-party remotes; sticking with one of Roku's official options should get you better support and features. Whatever you choose, verify that it's going to be compatible with your particular TV or streamer.

It has been revealed that if you've run through all of the above steps short of replacing your remote, one remaining option is to restart it. If it uses replaceable batteries, take them out, then press any two buttons before reinserting the batteries, negative sides first. If it uses a built-in battery, hold down its physical pairing controls (see the last section) for 20 seconds.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, there's not much else you can try short of clearing the cache on your Roku or updating or rebooting your Roku device, or you could learn how to reset your Roku. Be warned that if you try a reset, you'll have to reconfigure everything as if it were right out of the box. It's also unlikely to solve a green light concern, since as we've established, that's normally related to battery levels or pairing, not buggy software.

If worst comes to worst, you may be stuck using your phone for control. One pro tip, though — you don't always have to use the Roku app. If your setup supports AirPlay from iPhone or MacBook to your TV or screen mirroring on Roku with your Android phone, you can often cut to the chase with whatever audio or video it is you're trying to play.

#138745. Industry News: Why data centers are at the center of the Substantial Tech backlash

Industry News: Why data centers are at the center of the Substantial Tech backlash

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In his latest book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
  • Recent findings suggest that the book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections.
  • In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In his latest book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.

Recent findings suggest that the book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections. And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power.

In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”.

Recent findings suggest that “It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx mentioned. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”.

He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”.

During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.

I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?

Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.

Recent findings suggest that I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.

Sources indicate that obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these significant fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.

In a recent development, then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.

Industry observers note that it was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.

According to recent reports, before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?

Industry observers note that I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago, where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.

And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity, and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.

In a recent development, and then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant.

That was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention.

You don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now.

Absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable.

They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed.

I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies, but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do.

And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious with generative AI and the data centers to power them, where many of the benefits that were supposed to come of generative AI do not appear to have materialized — whether those are the economic benefits, the productivity benefits, but also the the benefits of delivery of services like healthcare and education to the public, as we heard Sam Altman saying a lot in the in the early days of ChatGPT.

Paired with that, there has been this massive environmental cost […] but there’s also this massive and growing social cost, when you think about the mental health impacts of chatbot dependence, of all the false information that pervades social media platforms now, of the deepfake crisis, and I could go on and on and on.

It’s not surprising that there has been backlash. But I have been surprised at how widespread it’s been, and also how bipartisan — you talk about Ron DeSantis and Bernie Sanders both being opposed to data centers. Why do you think it’s become such a unifying issue?

Because it’s not an abstract problem, right? I think even when we think about generative AI or social media or something like that, [it] can feel abstract. It’s a service that you access from your phone or from your computer. It’s not something that is tangible in the world.

But when a data center is coming to set up shop in your community, it’s very physical, it’s very material. It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on. You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.

It has been revealed that I think that there was already a pre-existing frustration with the tech industry that came from the quality of the products, the effects that they’re having on our society and our lives. For some people, [they have] frustration with the way that the tech industry has been collaborating with the Trump administration and with right-wing political groups in different parts of the world. But then you add on top of that the actual effects that come of having one of these infrastructures be planned or located in your community, and that anger gets kind of directed into that physical manifestation of this thing that you have an issue with.

In a recent development, obviously, the data centers are at the forefront of this, and it’s what we pay the most attention to. But we also see this increasingly with other aspects of the tech industry, whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.

There’s a lot of frustration with the physical manifestations of the tech industry, because that is something that can really be felt more directly, but can also be challenged more directly. You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the organization? It doesn’t often seem like very much.

Industry observers note that the tech companies have reacted to this backlash in a few different ways. One is that Microsoft, Amazon, and  OpenAI have all talked about [their commitment] that they’re not going to use NDAs anymore in their negotiations with local governments. How big a difference do you think that will make?

I do think it’s going to be good that it will be easier for people to access information on these projects that are being located in their communities. But part of the reason why we’re seeing these shifts is exactly in response to that opposition.

In a recent development, we’re seeing the tech companies propose to pay for more of the electricity infrastructure that will be required for their data centers to reduce the pressure on ratepayers, because people are angry about that. They’re promising to use different water-based cooling systems in their data centers, to say that they’re able to use less electricity.

When we look at the NDAs and the decision or the announcement that they’re not going to use those anymore, I think it’s also because it’s working against them. People know what a data center is now, and if people find out that a data center is coming to town and they have questions and they’re not getting answers, that’s only going to further fuel the opposition to those data centers.

Industry observers note that so, it’s not really a surprise to see [the tech companies] do this, and it’s a way that they can get a positive PR thing by saying, “We’re not going to use these NDAs that are working against us anyway. “.

One of the other ways they’ve responded is by saying that there’s a lot of misinformation about the environmental harms, or that they’re being overstated, or that they can mitigate them with renewable technology. How valid do you think those arguments are?

I think that the industry recognizes that there is a lot of concern and they’re trying to basically move into the discussion with narratives of their own to have people question whether data centers are really a problem or not.

I feel like we don’t see the industry doing as much on the energy side anymore, particularly on the fossil fuel side, because they realize that they have kind of lost that argument. If you look back a year and a half, two years ago, they were talking a lot about renewables, about nuclear energy, you don’t hear so much of that discourse anymore.

According to recent reports, they have pivoted, instead, to focus on the water question, where I think that they feel that they can use more abstract national figures in order to confuse the public about what’s going on. They can say, “If you look nationally, agriculture and golf courses also use a lot of water. So you don’t need to be worried about a data center coming to tow,n because they don’t use as much, in aggregate.”.

It has been revealed that but the issue with data center water use is not a national issue. It’s a local issue. There are unquestionably going to be communities where they seek to locate data centers that are going to have plenty of water and that are not going to be concerned about a data center coming to town. But they’re also locating [data centers] in a lot of communities that are experiencing high degrees of water stress, which means that they don’t have the water to really provide to these infrastructures.

We have also seen them pivoting to move away from the evaporative cooling systems, the ones that require a lot of water — because you need to take in a certain amount of water as it gets too hot, it evaporates away, and so you can see why you need a consistent flow of water into the data center for that type of cooling system —  to a closed loop system, where you basically have a certain amount of water, it stays within the data center, you keep cooling it down by using electricity to do that, and so you clearly don’t need as much water.

It has been revealed that that is their latest way to say, “Hey, don’t worry about the water use. We’re going to switch to this other system.” But the issue there, of course, is that it does require more electricity in order to keep that water cooled down, and that is often not part of what they talk about or discuss when they are proposing that as an alternative.

According to recent reports, then the other thing is that it’s not just water that is in those pipes or tubes going through the data center. There’s also a lot of coolant in there, a lot of chemicals, and communities where these projects are being located with closed loop cooling systems are becoming increasingly concerned about those coolants leaking out into their water supply and what that is going to mean.

In the book, you say repeatedly that you’re not against technology itself or even data centers in general, but [against] this hyperscale approach. The book is called “Hyperscale.” The last chapter is called “Human Scale.” Why do you see scale as such an important part of the problem?

Because scale is what creates the pressures, whether those are the pressures on the communities or you know the pressures on our wider electricity system and whatnot.

I don’t think that the inherent problem is data centers, because we have had data centers for a long time, and sure, there have been occasional concerns about specific projects, but data centers as a whole have not been an glitch that the public has felt merited this degree of attention. So that is why I feel the hyperscale data center, and particularly the acceleration that we’ve seen in the expansion of the size of these hyperscale data centers, but also the number of data centers that these companies are building out, is notable in this moment.

Linked to that is not just the scale of the demand created by these hyperscale data centers, but also, what they are supposed to be powering? That is where the other disconnect lies. They’re demanding a lot, but if we were actually getting something good for it, this might be justified. I think that for a lot of people, and I feel like we see this reflected in polling, they’re not actually seeing the benefits from generative AI.

So then the question becomes: “Okay, we’re expending all of these resources, we’re pushing up emissions such that climate change is going to be accelerated just to build out all these data centers to meet the ambitions of generative AI that the tech companies have, but then we’re not actually getting much benefit out of that technology. So what are we actually doing here?”.

One other thing that really struck a chord with me was your description about how tech executives often talk about the future as if there’s [just one] inevitable future. The only thing that’s in question is how promptly we arrive there [and] who’s going to make the most money off of it.

According to recent reports, this is so vital for me, because I do feel like how we think about the future then shapes decisions that we make. The tech billionaires, they see the future in a certain way […] and I think that they have been very successful in getting us to buy into their vision of the future for the past several decades. But that does not mean that that is the only way that the future has to be.

We can imagine a very different kind of future, and that would mean that we place our resources in different places and actually develop technology in a different way, toward different outcomes, with different incentives driving that work.

There are interesting conversations happening in different parts of the world right now around things like digital sovereignty, getting off of these technologies from the U.S. tech companies. But in some cases, those conversations are quickly captured by industry in those different parts of the world to say, “Okay, we want to get off U.S. technology, but let’s have our local companies do effectively the same thing, and just let them do the same exploitative practices and make the money that the U.S. tech companies would be making.” And I don’t think that that is the right way forward.

Recent findings suggest that I also think that there is a role for public sector development of technology in a way that we’ve eschewed or even looked at skeptically for the past number of decades, because the idea was that technology had to be left to the private sector. What we’re starting to see in Europe is a bit more funding of public technology, in order to develop the services that government itself depends on, and I think that that is a good first step.

But especially when we’re looking at the Microsoft outage that happened just recently, and we’re looking at Google threatening schools with their access to Google search if they don’t accept Google AI tool, I think that there’s a real moment right now to put resources into developing something different, that doesn’t come from these major tech companies, and that hopefully can have much more public benefit than what these companies now provide us.
