    Sources indicate that darryl Campbell, you’re a journalist, you’re an aviation expert, and you’re the author of the book Fatal Abstraction: Why the Managerial Class Loses Control of Software, which is potentially the most Decoder title in all of publishing history. Welcome to Decoder.

    In a recent development, thanks very much. Longtime listener, first-time caller. So thanks for having me.

    According to recent reports, I love that book title. I love all the ideas that it suggests. We’ll have you back to talk about the book, but I feel like we’re going to use that idea to talk about air traffic control today on Decoder with you.

    Sources indicate that yeah, I think so much of what we’ve found out, even in the week since my report came out, has really just been a lot of boring management failures that have somehow cascaded to affect millions of people on thousands of flights. And it’s just the importance of actually having people who know what they’re doing in charge.

    There’s a lot there already. There’s a whole hour of Decoder right there. But what you’re referencing is the fact that you wrote a story for us about the nationwide ground stop the FAA had to call because of a bad router. Tell us what we know. What happened here? Why did air traffic control ground you all?

    I’m going to take you back to Friday the 13th in a part of the country that nobody really associates with aviation, which is a little place called El Dorado, Arkansas. It’s the very tail end of part of this significant backbone of data and telecommunications that’s really a private network run exclusively for air traffic control by a company called L3Harris, who runs it on behalf of the FAA.

    According to recent reports, they’re just going in there, and they’re replacing what is essentially like 50-year-old infrastructure. If you remember back in the ‘90s, early 2000s when you made your first switch from DSL to fiber optic, that is exactly what they’re trying to do there, except-.

    So just to remind everybody, DSL ran on the phone lines.

    Yeah, so this is like a cable modem. So I’m old enough to remember that, and maybe some of you out there are. But yeah, this is like as soon as you plug in fiber, your speeds get five to 10 times faster. And that sounds great, but in the private telecom world, that happens on entirely separate networks.

    Recent findings suggest that your DSL provider isn’t your fiber provider, or if they are, they’re running on parallel networks. The FAA system has to do both at the same time, and so you have to figure out how we get all of these different cables, different routers, different protocols for how these things transmit data to all play nice with the same reliability and uptime? Because you need that when you’re managing tens of thousands of flights every single day.

    One of the things that I think is really key to understand here is that the FAA runs its own private network. It’s called the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure. It was built by this contractor back in the ‘90s and early 2000s. So it’s old, and it is actually due to be replaced, correct?

    Industry observers note that yeah, and that’s part of the challenge, because you have to have it to keep the aviation system going; you can’t just shut it down for a week, rip everything out, and replace it. So they’ve been doing piecemeal upgrades over time, and a lot of it is done by this L3Harris contractor, who’s one of the biggest defense companies in the world. They’ve been working with the FAA for a long time. You would think that they would know how to do a simple router swap without causing everything to go down, but that’s exactly what happened on Friday.

    If you go back and look at everything that exactly caused the outage, it’s like a comedy of errors. No single thing would have caused the entire system to crash, but every little missed opportunity, failed connection, or decision that somebody made with no knowledge of what happens downstream from everything, really led to the point where all of a sudden the most congested airspace in the world could not figure out where the airplanes were. They couldn’t talk to people who are en route, and that’s a serious safety problem that could have put thousands of people at risk.

    Let’s work backwards from the actual precipitating incident, and then let’s talk about the government’s response to this crisis. So there’s a router swap that happens in Arkansas. In your story, you say they swapped in a fiber router for an old copper router, and that thing started sending out too many requests for the network it was connected to.

    So L3Harris is trying to replace what is essentially a telephone switch from the 1960s with a new modern fiber optic data router. And so they’re removing the cabling, they’re removing the switch, and replacing it.

    Now, if you’re on, let’s say, a perfectly modern networking system, and you’re switching out a fiber optic for a fiber optic line, the data routing is the same; the protocols that the routers use to communicate with each other are the same. Do you remember that DSL to fiber optic comparison we made? That’s not really an issue because everything can handle huge amounts of data with high throughput.

    When the manufacturer sends out these newly introduced routers, there’s a factory setting on it that indicates, “Okay, when you’re making a communication attempt for the first time, assume that you are doing it with a high-throughput fiber optic system.” L3Harris forgot to turn off that switch, and so as soon as they plug in-.

    It has been revealed that yeah, from what I can tell and from all the reports that have come out, that is literally it. So L3Harris has said, “Hey, we did what we were supposed to. The router manufacturer said everything was working as it’s supposed to. There was no problem with the machine. It’s just that someone forgot to say, ‘Hey, you’re connecting to an old system.’” So when it starts pinging what it thinks is a high-capacity fiber optic data network, it’s just sending thousands and thousands of communication requests.

    Now, on their own, and if this wasn’t a critical infrastructural system, it probably would have done what I compare to a FaceTime call with bad Wi-Fi. All these connection requests start displacing some of the normal data packets that come through the network, and you start losing a couple of data packets, and so maybe the image quality degrades, or the audio starts to skip or something like that. That’s fine if you’re just trying to talk to someone in a normal one-on-one setting.

    But again, this is the air traffic control system for the world’s largest air traffic network, and you really can’t have any kind of data lag. And so what pilots start to see is the air traffic control routing centers that handle the high-altitude airplanes, the ones who are in cruise control and whatever; first, they start seeing some transmission loss. Sometimes it’s a radio transmission that cuts out. Over time, it gets worse as this router keeps pinging the system and keeps blasting it with all of these connection requests that cause data loss.

    Recent findings suggest that and then that starts cascading. So it’s not just radio traffic. It then becomes radar data, too, and then it becomes so overwhelming that entire centers are going offline. At the peak of the crisis, when Secretary Sean Duffy decided to start this ground stop, 17 out of the 22 en route control centers around the country had gone dark, and they were unable to communicate with airplanes that were en route, or see where they were, without having to rely on a backup system.

    In a recent development, that strikes me as all very bad, and as we saw, there was a ground stop. Why did it take quite as long as it did for anyone to say what happened?

    I’m thinking about [Transportation Secretary] Sean Duffy and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and their, frankly, absurd press conferences where they were saying conflicting things back to back from one another. They were not ruling out cyber attacks. What happened there? Why did it take so long to come up with what seems like a simple explanation for a very complicated problem?

    Yeah, well, if it sounded like people didn’t know what they were talking about, it’s because they didn’t. If you remember back in, I think, February of 2025, Elon Musk going in there with DOGE and firing a couple hundred people at the FAA. Now, you remember at the time — and in fact, I wrote a piece about it for The Verge — they said, “These aren’t safety-critical people. These aren’t the radar technicians. They’re not air traffic controllers.” That was true. But what they were was network engineers, data technicians, telecom specialists. These are the people who would have been overseeing the work that L3Harris was doing, and they simply did not exist.

    Recent findings suggest that so there was a CNN report that came out about this trail of evidence, where usually what would happen is the contractor comes in with a router, and then an FAA technician meets them and oversees the work. They do some tests to make sure that everything is going okay and that nothing is going to disrupt the entire system. Everybody signs off, and then everyone goes home, and nobody really knows that anything happened.

    Sources indicate that well, guess what didn’t happen? The FAA technician did meet the contractor, but they didn’t oversee any of the work. The contractor didn’t say that they were done. They didn’t let the FAA know that they were going to start testing. All of these decisions and all of these theoretically simple, easy tasks related to basic good management and governance didn’t happen. By the time people figured out what was going on, we were already four hours into what was the worst ground stop since 9/11.

    How did we figure out what was going on?

    So eventually L3Harris started isolating parts of the data management system — basically taking routers offline. That’s why one of the initial reports came out and noted, “Oh, we think we’ve isolated the problem to a part of the country that spans Arkansas and Texas.” And then, just one by one, taking these routers dark, they eventually turned off the single router that had gone and started creating these connection requests.

    Once that was offline, which honestly took them until around 7:40PM or 8PM ET on Friday, they were able, almost instantaneously, to start getting data and radar connections back. And then they decided to release the ground stop at that point. But it was really just your classic IT debugging of turning things off and seeing if anything changed until they found the right one.

    That’s right. Turn it off, turn it back on again.

    In a recent development, I remarked I wanted to move backwards. You stepped back to DOGE. Elon Musk comes in with DOGE. He takes the chainsaw to bureaucracy. He fires a bunch of network technicians. It seems like a bunch of processes go out the window. But this is a long story, right? This is a rickety system that we’ve known needed to be upgraded for years. Is it really just DOGE that brought us to the brink of incompetence, or is there a story beyond that?

    Yeah, I think it’s not just years, but decades. I mean, the main problem is that the money, effort, and sustained attention required to do all of these kinds of boring network upgrades operate on time horizons that are like five to 10 years. Whereas in politics, your time horizon is maybe a year or two max, every time you’re going back to budgeting, to getting the political will to get things passed.

    Industry observers note that because those things are so far out of sync, number one, it’s hard to just get the money in the first place to do these expensive upgrades. Number two, keep the money going so that the project is perfectly budgeted and the contractors have started on it, then get the money to keep doing the work that they need to do for a couple of years. And then number three, to maintain that momentum across administrations, across congressional changes, and really across party shifts. That’s been the big problem — that whenever a sort of smaller government, anti-regulation administration comes in, they start cutting some of the funding, and usually the FAA is on the chopping block.

    It’s almost kind of ironic that pilots, air traffic controllers, and the people who operate the system behind the scenes have actually gotten so good at making up for the FAA and the air traffic control system’s flaws — just because their machines are literally falling apart — that we’ve kind of papered over some of the issues and gone around some of the problems. If these had surfaced maybe five or 10 years ago, maybe we would be a little bit faster about getting the upgrades that we need today.

    Just continuing the theme of moving backwards, it’s not as though people didn’t know, right? There was funding to modernize the system. That funding was controversial in the way that whenever Democrats pass funding and Republicans take power, the funding becomes controversial.

    Sources indicate that it’s funny. There’s a video of Sec. Duffy saying the Biden administration was wasting money that they should have been spending on the FAA. And then after this incident, he’s begging for $50 billion at a press conference. It seems like everyone knew about the problem, right? We have a blueprint to fix it. There’s a date to replace the system. Why isn’t there more urgency?

    Yeah, so I think there are two parts to your question here. I think number one is the political will required to get the budget in the first place, which is kind of like a two- to three-year process where you have to identify the company that can actually do the work. That’s part of the reason why we’ve got all these substantial incumbent defense companies because you can’t have some startup in San Francisco figure out how to change 3,000 miles of cabling overnight. That just can’t be done.

    Sources indicate that and then you have to go through the work of getting it passed through Congress, through all of the accountability layers like the Government Accountability Office and all of the other procedural guardrails that are designed to keep government waste somewhat under control. That’s largely good, except that by the time we get the reports and actually figure out, okay, here’s what we need to do, here’s the right vendor, and so on, usually that’s after a midterm or after an administration change, and the political will has already kind of gone out the window.

    Sources indicate that so I think that’s one part of it. And I think the second part is the FAA is just kind of suffering from death by a thousand cuts over the last 20, 30, 40 years. Even if they do the right thing, which is that they should be replacing a lot of these older switches with latest routers, by the time that happens, all of the other challenges with the administration and the agency have kind of filtered down to the point where they just don’t have the people in place.

    Industry observers note that let’s say you’re a network engineer who really knows their stuff and who could be in the right place for it. After three to five years of just sort of will they, won’t they, am I going to have a job next year, and all of the other things that get in the way of you being able to do your job, you’re probably going to go into private industry at that point. So I think there’s a talent problem and there’s this kind of overall political problem that’s really causing a lot of these concerns.

    Recent findings suggest that I want to rewind to the beginning of the second Trump administration, which feels like 10 million years ago, but it was not so long ago. It was two years ago. Elon comes in with DOGE; he’s got the chainsaw for bureaucracy, and he’s firing these people. He’s maybe getting rid of some of the talent you’re talking about.

    But there’s also a bunch of aviation catastrophes that happened, right? Planes were crashing, there were near misses at airports, and we heard a lot about how, because Elon was in the government, we would instantly modernize our infrastructure. We were going to rip Verizon out and replace it with Starlink. We were going to AI vibe code all the software. Did anything come of that, or did anything happen because of that?

    In a recent development, A couple of things have happened, but not to the extent that they’re addressing some of the major problems with the system. I think the biggest challenge here, and it’s kind of a quirk of the U.S. air traffic control system, is that our regulator and also the entity that operates all of the infrastructure and air traffic control systems are one and the same.

    It’s actually quite a hard thing for, in particular, Republicans and small government conservatives to get the idea that it’s good to fund the FAA when, in their mind, it’s a regulator as much as it is kind of the operator. That already creates a lot of challenges.

    I think the second thing that we talk about, and specific to DOGE, was that a lot of the contracts that they gave out were from people in that Silicon Valley orbit. So you think about Palantir; there’s a upcoming company called ASI that’s now running the SMART AI air traffic control system.

    Recent findings suggest that yeah, that’s been kind of a substantial conspiracy theory thing. But those are great, and they’re important systems, but the biggest challenges for the FAA are physical in nature. How do we replace this gigantic network? How do we get these telephone switches out of the ground and replace them with fiber optics? How do we replace radar and communications technology that is, in some cases, literally held together with duct tape and aluminum foil? And that part you’re never going to be able to do as kind of a small startup operating entirely in the digital and software space.

    According to recent reports, I mean, the people that they gave contracts to and the people that benefited the most were attacking some small part of the problem, but not the one that’s related to how do you keep airplanes from not running into each other or how do you make sure that air traffic control radios are working so that helicopters don’t crash into commercial flights. Those are really hard, intractable, physical world problems that this sort of Silicon Valley AI vibe coding thing is never going to solve.

    There was some amount of drama about Verizon being ripped out and replaced with Starlink. The idea that we could just upgrade the networks and equip all the planes with latest sensors — there was energy around that in the beginning of the Trump administration. It appears to have just completely fizzled.

    It’s part of this contractual incumbent thing. You can say whatever you want about replacing a vendor you don’t like with the one from your buddy down the hall, but it’s going to take years. Verizon, I think, did get moved out of some contracts, but they were replaced with another big telecom firm, not Starlink.

    I mean, I’m pretty sure that there’s one Starlink system, and it’s operating in the middle of nowhere in Alaska. So on paper, yeah, Starlink has something, but again, they’re just not equipped to handle some of the massive problems with all of this sort of legacy cabling and networking.

    In a recent development, you mentioned your buddy’s company down the hall. That brings us directly to ASI, which is the center of one of the hottest conspiracy theories about the ground stop that exists. Sean Duffy’s son, Michael Alfonso, is running for office. ASI contributed to his campaign.

    People have drawn this connection. They think there’s some sort of kickback, but ASI was hired to implement some AI-based system, or SMART system, that was going on while the ground stop happened. Are these things connected in any way?

    Sources indicate that in a word, no. A lot of the conspiracy theories that have come up around this SMART system really came about in this gray space because the messaging from the administration was so bad, and there’s this natural antipathy towards AI. But all that SMART is doing is replacing some of the manual printouts and the routing that happens at the level of air traffic controllers in sort of control towers and facilities.

    It has been revealed that they’re not actually plugged into the data backbone. They’re not handling any of the radar or the sensitive radio data. They’re just kind of a parallel system operating out in space. Now that being said, it’s because you’ve got the Secretary of Transportation and the Secretary of Homeland Security out there kind of shooting from the hip at their press conference that inspired exactly zero confidence in the messaging that they were giving.

    It has been revealed that to give him a little bit of credit, Sean Duffy did say a couple of accurate things, but the way that he mentioned them and then literally in the next sentence walked it back and said, “But it could be 10 other things,” does not inspire confidence at all. I think networking is a hard thing to explain to your average person because their eyes may glaze over, and then you have someone who really doesn’t understand it, who’s trying to do the right thing. But in his mind, the main point of that whole press conference was to get to that $30 or $50 billion shakedown of the government. So he’s kind of blowing past the technical details in the first place.

    It was just not a great look, and I think that’s why some of this conspiracy theory stuff has started to thrive.

    You mentioned the natural antipathy towards AI. Obviously, this ground stop happened in the context of many other outages. Microsoft Outlook went down. United had an problem that brought it down for several hours. There were other outages this week. There was a Chase Bank outage that people overread into thinking it was a banking system outage.

    There’s a lot of AI antipathy out there. There’s a lot of, “Well, this must be either AI-powered cyber attacks or everyone’s vibe coding garbage software and pushing into production; it’s crashing.” The top comment on your story is, “I call BS on this. It was AI, but we won’t hear it. They’re using this to beg for money they need after Elon Musk tore air traffic control apart.” Is there an AI element to this story at all?

    I would say to that commentary that it gets two out of the three, so that’s pretty good. The AI component, I think, is really more about what happens in three to five years when we fully transition, I’m sure, to this AI-powered system. I think that’s the part where we’re really going to see how good it is.

    According to recent reports, right now, air traffic controllers are still using legacy processes to route planes and keep track of everything. And those processes work pretty well. I mean, I’ve talked with hundreds of air traffic controllers over the years. They’re uniformly professional, very skilled, and more importantly, they know the ways that their systems will break down so that when something happens, they can immediately figure out how to keep things going without putting everybody at risk.

    According to recent reports, when you do eventually move to the SMART AI system, that’s going to be a whole unknown. And I think that’s really kind of where my concern would be: when they turn it on for a larger portion of the air traffic control system, where they say, “Okay, from now on,” I’m just making this up, “Chicago is going to be on the SMART system, and we’ll see what happens.” That’s the day that maybe I would avoid flying for a little while.

    I don’t have the data to back this up, but it just feels like flying has gotten more chaotic and dangerous in the second Trump administration than before. There have been more crashes. Is that related to management incompetence? Is that just a string of bad luck?

    Chaotic for sure. I think dangerous, probably not. I mean, if you think about the incentives that line up, airlines do not want to have a crash. Passengers don’t want to fly on something dangerous. So with whatever’s going on at the administration level, there’s enough pushback within industry and within the passenger market that nobody is really going to take steps that they think will actively degrade the system.

    That being said, I would say you’re 100 percent justified in thinking that you should be less confident in the regulation and operations leadership side today than you would be five years ago. You heard it on Friday night and Saturday morning that the people in charge don’t really care what’s going on, and they just want the optics to look good. Even if you push them on the details, the people who knew what they were doing are really not in place anymore. I think we’ll probably see more of these disruptions over the next couple of years. I don’t think we’ll ever see anything that gets to the point of being materially more unsafe.

    In large part, I think the ground stop was probably justified. I mean, I talked to a bunch of controllers who said, “We could have handled it. We could have gone to backup systems, and in 20, 30, 40 minutes, things would’ve been more or less back to normal.” And I believe them. I think they absolutely could have handled some of these outages without causing any real safety risks.

    But from a passenger standpoint, you also don’t want to hear, and that’s part of the reason I started the story with that anecdote, “Hey, this is your pilot. We can’t communicate with anybody. We’re going to kind of see how it goes.” That is a very scary thing to hear.

    I think that really fuels a lot of it: that any kind of perceived safety risk in aviation just awakens this primordial fear in people. That’s totally justified. And I think it helps keep some of these anti-regulation impulses in check because people know that once a critical mass of people are afraid of flying, you kind of undo an industry that holds the entire United States and, in many respects, the world together.

    One of the things that’s really interesting about this dynamic, this whole story, is that if you were to design an air traffic control system from scratch today, it would be vastly more automated, right?

    Industry observers note that you would absolutely have an enormous amount of computer control over where the airplanes are. You would build vastly more powerful communication between planes and air traffic control centers in between them, and you would maybe even just let ATC control the planes directly, right?

    According to recent reports, it’s a closed ecosystem where everyone wants to participate and has aligned incentives. You would just say, “Okay, the robots are going to fly all the planes for us, and they’re going to be perfectly safe.” But it doesn’t seem like there’s a pathway from here to there.

    At least not in the United States. I think there are so many counterarguments to some of the good intentions that people have, and frankly, a lot of people are just trying to get in because they want a hand of the government payout pie. I would be very worried if someone said, “Hey, tomorrow we’re going to launch robot planes coming out of Atlanta.”.

    According to recent reports, I do think a potential competing model is what we see in China, where they don’t have some of these competing economic or political gamesmanship kind of counterforces going on, where they are able to build what is essentially a fresh air traffic control system largely from scratch and with updated technology. And I think we are seeing some of the ways that automation is making that more efficient.

    It has been revealed that that being mentioned, I would bet you $100 that would never happen in the US, at least not until something materially changes in the way that the US thinks about air travel. I mean, we think about it as a right. We think about it as the primary way that we get from point A to point B other than driving a car for 100 miles, and we think about it as something that everybody should have access to.

    So, that means we want it cheap, we want it fast, and we’re kind of able to tolerate some of these large-scale disruptions as long as it doesn’t affect our Thanksgiving intends in a week. I think that also just kind of keeps the system the way it is in ways that maybe are not the case in some other countries that are newer to large-scale aviation.

    I like that you made reference to the cliché: you can have it cheap, fast, or good. Now pick two.

    In a recent development, that’s what you’re saying. In this case, maybe none.

    Industry observers note that there’s another argument I’ve heard, and this is in Project 2025. You mentioned the industry has a lot of incentives to figure this out, to make it good, to make sure people feel safe. In Project 2025, the idea that we should privatize air traffic control exists.

    According to recent reports, at the beginning of the second Trump administration, as Elon was slashing air traffic control and the FAA, the notion that this would lead inexorably to privatized air traffic control that could then impose a bunch of this stuff, because the industry would be doing it to itself, was everywhere. I heard about it constantly. That doesn’t seem to have happened. Is there a push, is there an argument to be made for private air traffic control?

    We definitely saw that, and I think with Project 2025, that’s been a plank of The Heritage Foundation’s blueprint for government for more than two decades, if not since the late ‘80s when Reagan fired the air traffic controllers.

    I think privatization is a difficult concept for a lot of people to get their head around. But I do think the core idea, which is that you kind of need to separate the FAA as regulator from FAA as air traffic control operator, is fundamentally sound, whether that means moving it into a new government department or some other structural change.

    A lot of places around the world do have privatized air traffic control, so Canada, the UK, Germany, or they have a different system entirely. In Brazil, for example, air traffic control is actually controlled by the military.

    China is really the only big country that has a similar structure, but when you’re in a one-party system, it doesn’t really function as it does in the US. That is kind of a weird quirk that needs to be solved one way or another.

    The quirk is that the regulator also oversees air traffic control.

    Industry observers note that correct. But I just don’t know what the right pathway is because there’s also… I mean, you’re seeing it today with some of these contractors who are coming in and essentially scamming the government about everything, and that doesn’t seem to me like a safe way to operate the air traffic control system. How do you compensate for that human/corporate nature that we seem to have here, where you do kind of want to maximize profits even past the point of producing a good product?

    In a recent development, the airline industry is not full of shy characters. Ed Bastian, the CEO of Delta, is not a reserved figure. These are big personalities; they run big businesses, they battle with each other, and they spend enormous amounts of money. As you said, they’re the backbone of the global economy in many ways. Why can’t they push for it? Why aren’t they leading the charge?

    It has been revealed that ah, so there’s an interesting one. They are leading the charge publicly, while in private not really committing any considerable support to it. So let me put this in the context of aviation security. It costs the US government about $10 to screen for baggage, security, and whatever. But if you look at your airline ticket, your average FAA 9/11 fee, whatever it’s called today, is $1.50. That was because airlines pushed so hard against any kind of thing that would increase their fares that we’re essentially losing money on every security scan.

    Now, whether or not security works is a whole other story, but that’s kind of the mentality that they have. It’s great for them to pontificate about what we need, but if you ask the airlines to shoulder some of the burden, they’re going to say, “Well, this is going to blow up our entire economic model.” That’s a difficult thing to swallow.

    I mean, in Canada, they just make them pay for the fees. The security fee is about 10 times higher. The fees for their private air traffic control system also pass through to the passengers, but that means that they don’t have your $70 “go somewhere cheap this weekend” kind of fares that we do in the US. So there are trade-offs, and I think the industry isn’t yet willing to part with some of that margin in order to upgrade the air traffic control system. They think it should be a government burden to pay.

    If the listener is keeping track of us going backwards, we started with one router that was replaced with a misconfigured setting, and we’ve arrived at how we should split up the FAA and change the fee structure for airlines. That is a long and winding road, but it feels like a very direct connection.

    It has been revealed that yeah, absolutely. I mean, these kinds of changes take decades to do. If you’re in that short-term mentality, that one where you’re just trying to make it to the next election or you just need this particular line on the budget, you’re never going to get to a world where we can have a fully functional air traffic system.

    Sources indicate that part of the thing is that people do hide behind this complexity to both extract money from the government funds that are available or to just be able to… Case in point, Sec. Duffy, who, when he was a congressman, voted against funding for the FAA. Now six, seven, eight years later, he’s saying, “Oh my gosh, what a terrible idea. Whoever did that in the first place should be banned from the government. By the way, I also need $50 billion more to do it.”.

    You can kind of see how short-term memory, the political cycle, and everything else line up to make sure that we kind of get the system we deserve in a way.

    Let’s say Sec. Duffy was massively competent. He was the single best network design engineer that has ever existed. This is a lot for a cast member of The Real World, but so it goes. What if you gave him $50 billion? If you dumped $50 billion on the FAA today, could it accomplish building a system that was reliable, stable, much more automated, and safer?

    It has been revealed that I think it could happen in a couple of years, but it’s not just the money that you would need. I think you would need a couple of other things too. Number one, you just have to have the managers who can do it. So you remember Mark Zuckerberg; his whole thing was like, “Let’s get rid of all these middle managers.” But they have a function. And especially when you’re dealing with legacy systems, complex technical installations, and the management of just large networks of people, not just data, but people.

    Recent findings suggest that you kind of need those people who are in these glue functions to make sure that, hey, maybe let’s not do something on a Friday afternoon when even a small failure is going to bring down a busy air traffic controller. Maybe let’s have a initiative that says, hey, let’s check the factory settings when you plug in this thing.

    The thing that gives me confidence is that we’ve done it so far, even in these conditions where we’re not having massive numbers of crashes, and that we are willing to pause the system when it makes sense to do so. But you can only go on for so long like that.

    I think we’ll get through Thanksgiving.

    [Laughs] That was a long pause, dude.

Now people are on guard for that. And from what we’ve heard from the FAA, they’re not installing any new routers anytime soon. That particular risk is pretty much eliminated.

    I would say your safety has never really been at risk, and people are still able to manage these crises when they happen. So I wouldn’t worry about safety. I would say give yourself a couple of extra hours either way.

    For example, I flew to Boston over this past weekend. Saturday morning, even though the ground stop had been lifted, we were still delayed over an hour. It was not because of any communications problem, but because so many things had happened to put airplanes and people out of place that they were literally calling flight attendants on their day off to come in and work, and that’s what my aircraft was waiting for.

    In a recent development, recovery will happen. Disruptions can be managed to a certain extent. But I think if we get to another year from now and we’re still paralyzed in this world of, “Well, let’s just spend the time pointing fingers rather than doing anything meaningful,” then I think it really starts to call into question whether we do have the capacity to fix what’s wrong with the air traffic system.

    Sources indicate that FTI, the network at problem here, is due to be replaced in 2028. Just to wrap it up, what are the markers you’re looking for to see if that process is happening as intended and we are going to wind up with a better, more reliable network?

    One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

    In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who mentioned they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

While this price tier can sometimes be challenging to shop for — caught between affordable accessories and significant-ticket items — there’s plenty of gold to be mined for clever shoppers. And we’re here to help.

    In a recent development, this guide includes a wide range of cool finds at $50 or less, from mainstream hits like KPop Demon Hunters on Blu-ray and popular tech like the DJI Mic Mini to more eccentric picks like VidaBay’s E Ink fridge magnets and the Werewolf USB-C power adapter.     If someone on your list collects Game Boy, Game Boy Color, or Game Boy Advance cartridges, the GB Operator might be the perfect gift. The slick, transparent USB-C device makes it easy to play and manage classic titles on a macOS or Windows machine via emulation, with or without achievements.

Its carrying case houses all the accessories needed to get that sweet shot of bean, making real coffee available virtually anywhere.

The slow-burning LP is gorgeously recorded and delightfully weird, and it feels tailor-made for vinyl, making it an easy pick for Harding fans (or anyone who loves quirky indie jams).

    Rechargeable AA batteries are great for the environment and your budget, but not all models are created equally, so we did our own testing. With top-tier capacity, breezy usability, and a compact USB-C charging case, Zepath’s batteries are the best we’ve tried.

    Recent findings suggest that give the gift of security with this USB-C smart camera, which offers a wide field of view, night vision, microSD storage, and free Wi-Fi livestreaming. The optional subscription adds cloud storage and smart object detection, letting customers upgrade as needed.

    Sources indicate that moft’s origami-inspired “invisible” stand provides a sleek way to prop up your tablet or laptop (up to 14 inches) and to keep your working space looking more organized. The design has features like ventilation gaps and firm grips to work on a variety of surfaces and devices.

    Recent findings suggest that this affordable dongle kit provides an almost magical way to power nearly any DC device from a USB-C charger or portable battery. Program it from a mobile app, connect it to your old gear, then everything from a PC monitor to an original Game Boy can accept USB-C charging.

    Hoto’s electric screwdriver is a thoughtful gift for the builder in your life. The compact, easy-to-use tool includes 12 S2 steel bits, a circular LED to illuminate your project, and a soft, yet grippy handle. Three torque settings allow for a variety of jobs, and a long-lasting battery (with USB-C charging) keeps the driver going for hours.

    In a recent development, it can be hard to keep in touch with friends, but Major Walk might be the game that gets the gang back together. The cooperative multiplayer title drops players into a wacky world as spherical humanoids who must solve puzzles by chatting and teaming up. You’ll want at least two copies, and sessions support up to 12 players.

    Sources indicate that this handy Japanese organizer is a thoughtful gift for folks who prefer a physical way to keep track of everything, from upcoming events and projects to random thoughts and creative ideas. It comes in multiple sizes and can be customized with artistic covers in a variety of colors and designs. Take your pick.

    SwitchBot’s futuristic block, which is designed to activate physical switches from afar, is as useful as it is eccentric. Also available in a rechargeable configuration, the app-controllable button pusher clips onto almost anything with a switch and lasts up to 600 days on a single 3V CR2 battery.

    Everyone needs a basic toolkit, and Ron Swanson would agree. I’m not sure he’d go for the micro-sized set from iFixit, but we can back it. It’s an excellent entry point for folks living in small homes or apartments. Headlined by a 32-bit screwdriver set, it includes two pairs of tweezers, dual spudgers, and more.

    It has been revealed that easySMX makes our favorite Nintendo Switch 2 controllers, and the S10 Lite adds a major upgrade: native system functionality. The Lite skips a few features, like amiibo support and high-quality rumble, but otherwise provides a solid value for those on a budget.

    Sources indicate that as any experienced content creator will tell you, capturing good audio is more than half the battle. DJI’s Mic Mini gives aspiring creators a leg up with a sleek mic and transmitter set, enabling up to 10 hours of recording time, plus powerful noise canceling to capture the narrative, not the unwanted noise.

    This collapsible stand converts your Steam Deck or Switch 2 into a desktop-like experience. It includes cable guides and works with Mechanism’s accessories for attaching battery banks and more.

    These self-looping USB-C cables from SuperCalla might be just what your gift recipient needs. Instead of flat cables that often become unwieldy, these are capped with slim magnetic threads that stick together in a tight coil, making cable organization a breeze.     So what if you’ve heard “Golden” more times than you can count? Netflix’s massive animated hit is a lot easier to gift now that it’s officially available on 4K Blu-ray disc. The story about three pop stars who band together to save humanity from a demonic boy band is an instant classic, with fantastic music and striking animation.

    Industry observers note that these nifty fridge magnets might revolutionize grandma’s refrigerator. Designed to look like Polaroid pictures, they each feature an E-Ink screen and NFC communication, letting owners easily upload fresh photos to the frame by simply tapping their phones on them. It feels like magic, but it’s just a really cool application of some modern tech.

    Sure. You could put iced tea in them, but no one’s stopping you from sipping pulpy OJ or rich chocolate milk from Kinto’s stylish glassware, which was crafted with an “uninterfering design” in mind. Needless to say, a full set makes a lovely addition to any minimalist’s ensemble.

    Let your loved ones sling their new Apple gear safely and in style with these official, well-made Apple Wrist Straps. Compatible with AirPods Pro 2 and iPhone 17 cases or newer, they’re a practical way to carry phones and earbuds when pockets won’t do.

    It has been revealed that this durable handheld system for preschoolers and up is the perfect gift for your favorite budding gamer.     Industry observers note that while Zepath’s batteries are the top AA rechargeables we’ve tested, Paleblues are a convenient alternative for those after USB-C charging on each cell instead of in a case. They come with a four-headed cable to charge a four-pack from a single USB-C port.

    In a recent development, for the person on your list whose hatred for smart glasses runs deep, Knockaround’s hip, tech-free sunglasses should hit the spot.     Sources indicate that bring Nintendo’s popular Mario Kart racing game to life with this collectible RC car. Beyond the kart, the package includes a jewel display case, a controller and batteries, and can be accompanied by rivals like Toad, Luigi, Peach, and Yoshi. Race on!

    For your next Secret Santa gift swap at work or in your friend group, we submit this zany head-shaped lamp from Ikea. Its color-changing profile looks cool, so long as you don’t mind having a head as decor. Beyond that, it provides a useful way to store items like hats and sunglasses.

    Sources indicate that in the age of remote work, you can get the job done from just about anywhere at home. With this clever laptop desk, your favorite worker can easily log on from bed or on the couch without having to awkwardly prop their machine on a throw pillow. It offers adjustable legs, a foldable design, and a nonslip surface.

    According to recent reports, let your favorite gamer turn their phone into a Game Boy, of sorts. 8BitDo’s controller pad emulates Nintendo’s classic handheld and slides directly into your phone’s USB-C port, perfect for emulation. It offers a soft backpad that won’t scratch your screen, and its hinged connector lets it detach with ease.

    CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler for $44 billion

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies unveiled Monday.
    • Crowdstrike and Zscaler mentioned that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.
    • Zscaler is a San Jose, Calif.-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies unveiled Monday.

    Crowdstrike and Zscaler mentioned that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.

    Zscaler is a San Jose, Calif.-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.

    CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones and other devices connected to a tech giant’s network, noted the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers.

    In remarks on Monday, the companies stated that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI.

    The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.

    Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded.

    Sources indicate that multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

    Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterwards.

    “I spoke to them, let me put it that way… And I convinced them,” the president told CNBC.

    Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report.

    According to recent reports, “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor.

    The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to remark that, “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.”.

    According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the manufacturer claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

    While Trump has declared that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet.

    It has been revealed that “People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump noted to CNBC.

    Trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even denying that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The New York Times reported, on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May.

    Earlier this spring, Rubio also supervised the drafting of a memo which circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security.

    #138649. Industry News: Jensen Huang isn’t out of the woods yet

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (855 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Jensen Huang isn’t out of the woods yet

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services.
    • Still, tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang’s reinstatement.
    • In a recent development, most importantly, serious questions remain about how Nvidia chips were smuggled into China, and how much Nvidia knew about it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s safe to say no one expected this.

    Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services. With so much of the AI industry built on top of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure, Huang’s departure looked like an imminent threat to the business — and the mood on his return has been ecstatic. Share prices are rocketing back up, particularly for neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and the Nasdaq rose 7% on the news.

    Still, tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang’s reinstatement. President Trump is already telling reporters that the US government found no national security concerns resulting from the affair, but the broader national security concerns aren’t so easy to dismiss, and Trump’s involvement may do more harm than good for Nvidia and its partners. This isn’t the end of the problems caused by Huang’s affairs; it’s likely just the beginning.

    In a recent development, most importantly, serious questions remain about how Nvidia chips were smuggled into China, and how much Nvidia knew about it. Among Jensen Huang’s defenders, it’s become common to question whether Alice Huang was really a spy, but it’s clear that a lot of restricted chips were flowing into China through her company. Just this weekend, the Fresh York Times reported sustained contact between Alice Huang and a member of China’s Ministry of State Security during the same period she was having an affair with Jensen Huang.

    With Democrats in control of Congress, including investigative bodies like the House Oversight Committee, there are plenty of ways to force the issue. Nvidia’s role in violating US export controls would likely have been the subject of prolonged uncomfortable investigation, whether Huang returned or not. But with him back in the CEO’s seat, there will be a lot more riding on any revelations that come up — and any new revelations will damage Nvidia as a manufacturer alongside Huang himself.

    Then there are the questions raised by the pardon itself. It’s unprecedented in American history for a sitting president to intervene to clear a CEO accused of being a national security risk. Simply pressing the Department of Justice to exonerate Huang would have been a scandal, but calling the Nvidia board goes significantly further. Huang has already donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project, so it’s easy to make the case that Trump was intervening on behalf of a donor, setting national security risks aside for his personal benefit.

    Recent findings suggest that all of this is happening just as Democrats retake Congress, with all of its associated investigative powers. Even if they can’t fire Huang or remove Trump, there are lots of uncomfortable questions that are still unanswered. Was there any Department of Justice inquiry into whether Huang had committed a crime, or did Trump make the call on his own? Did the intelligence services make any official assessment that could be subpoenaed into the congressional record? Investigating Democrats will be particularly interested in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees export controls and retains significant financial ties to the industry through his firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.

    According to recent reports, if all of this sounds exhausting, you’re getting a sense of what the next year will be like for anyone following national news. Congress will keep a steady drip of embarrassing revelations, milking as much political juice as possible out of Huang and everyone associated with him. Trump will keep lashing out, often making things worse for everyone involved. (Trump’s statement to CBS, which defends Huang in racist terms while also accusing him of treason, is an early taste.) It’s going to be ugly and sad, and the most successful tech company of the last decade will be right at the center of it.

    I have to assume that this was the scenario the board was concerned about when it decided to remove Huang two weeks ago. Since then, the cost of removing him has gone up: an open letter from Nvidia’s employees and partners, a tanking stock market and, ultimately, direct intervention from the President of the United States.

    But nothing has lowered the cost of keeping Huang, and the ugly scenario the board foresaw earlier this month is still very much in place. We’re about to see it come to life.

    Trump also remarked, “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”.

    Nvidia noted in its announcement that its board “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that made them confident reinstating Huang would not pose a national security risk, following reports about his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.

    Trump also posted on Truth Social that Nvidia’s board “made the correct and proper decision” to reinstate Huang, adding:.

    According to recent reports, “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”.

    Less than 12 hours earlier, Trump said in a separate post that Huang’s reinstatement “would be the best thing” for Nvidia and the US, and urged the board to rehire him. Reporting from Semafor now indicates that he was calling into Nvidia’s board meeting around this time to make the same argument.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Umamusume: Pretty Derby is teaming up with the Denver Broncos for their clash against the Miami Dolphins, bringing Gold Ship and Mejiro McQueen to the NFL in specially designed uniforms.

    From appearing at the Grand Prix de Paris to being plastered across a BMW in Japan’s Super GT championship, Umamusume’s anime horse girls have been sighted at a lot of sports events this year.

    While the Seattle Seahawks previously shared Umamusume-inspired fan art on social media, the Denver Broncos are taking the crossover further with an official collaboration that brings both Gold Ship and Mejiro McQueen to their stadium for the December 6 game.

    During the game at Empower Field at Mile High, Umamusume will appear on the stadium’s screens and horseshoe-shaped LED ribbon.

    Fans attending the game could also find themselves on an Umamusume-themed fan cam, you know, just in case you were worried there weren’t enough horse girls in your soccer game.

    There’s even going to be life-size cutouts of Gold Ship and Mejiro McQueen available for photos at a booth near Gate 8. Visitors can collect a postcard featuring the pair and a rally flag showing Gold Ship’s touchdown, with both illustrations specifically created for the event.

    Industry observers note that we scored a collab with the Denver Broncos! 🏈At the Dec 6 home game, look out for Umamusume displays around the stadium, including life-sized standees of Gold Ship and Mejiro McQueen! And don't miss the goodies up for grabs!🥕https://t.co/cVaS2UCs2Z#BroncosUmamusume pic.twitter.com/nf1UIZk1JT.

    It’s crucial to note that you don’t need a game ticket to visit the Umamusume booth or receive the giveaways, but you will need one to watch the Denver Broncos take on the Miami Dolphins inside the stadium.

    The booth opens at 11:05 a.m. MST on December 6 and closes at 2:05 p.m., when the Broncos’ Week 13 game kicks off.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A woman has revealed that she completed seven marathons in 2026 despite being pregnant for a few of them, admitting that it was a bit “bizarre” at times.
    • Recent findings suggest that for a lot of people, running a marathon is a goal that they work towards for months, if not years.
    • In a recent development, in the case of Deirdre Keane, the 38-year-old is a seasoned long-distance runner, completing more than 60 marathons to this point.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A woman has revealed that she completed seven marathons in 2026 despite being pregnant for a few of them, admitting that it was a bit “bizarre” at times.

    Recent findings suggest that for a lot of people, running a marathon is a goal that they work towards for months, if not years. Some want to set an impressive time, while others just want to be able to say they’ve completed the 26.2 miles.

    In a recent development, in the case of Deirdre Keane, the 38-year-old is a seasoned long-distance runner, completing more than 60 marathons to this point. However, throughout 2026, she has been running marathons with an additional hurdle to deal with: she has been pregnant throughout.

    “I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point,” she told the Associated Press, admitting it is a “very unusual” challenge, but noted that she isn’t the first woman to do so.

    As per the AP, the 38-year-old had signed up for 11 races in 2026, including the seven major marathons: Berlin, Boston, Chicago, London, Fresh York, Sydney and Tokyo.

    Sources indicate that “I was like, this is going to be my last hurrah before settling down and becoming pregnant, becoming a mother,” Keane added. However, she didn’t discover she was pregnant until after running the Tokyo marathon, when she noticed her pace had started to slip.

    It has been revealed that “I don’t think she thought I would do them towards the end, especially being so pregnant at Newly introduced York. But I am very stubborn and determined,” Keane added. “Plus, I got lucky; I was feeling good. So I was able to do it.”.

    Elsewhere, an influencer was forced to apologize after cheating during the Berlin Marathon. Chinese creator Abeeeer was caught riding on the back of a bicycle despite celebrating her finish as a personal best time.

    According to recent reports, another influencer, Mike Clarke, was banned from the Newly introduced York Marathon after going viral for high-fiving Ariana Grande during the run. Clarke had never actually signed up for the marathon and used a counterfeit race number.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A university in China has rolled out a $5 million surveillance system that actually checks if people are paying attention in class.
    • Sources indicate that plenty of schools across the globe have embraced technology in their classrooms.
    • So, these days, it can be pretty difficult to slack off, not pay attention to what your teacher is saying, and then grab some notes from your friend.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A university in China has rolled out a $5 million surveillance system that actually checks if people are paying attention in class.

    Sources indicate that plenty of schools across the globe have embraced technology in their classrooms. Some of these have been as simple as letting kids use iPads and computers, while other schools are fully focused on teaching students about AI. Others are even using AI-powered robots to help them teach.

    So, these days, it can be pretty difficult to slack off, not pay attention to what your teacher is saying, and then grab some notes from your friend.

    Over in China, though, things have been taken to the next level when it comes to checking on who is actually paying attention to the lessons.

    As per the South China Morning Post, Nanjing University, in Jiangsu province, has rolled out a smart classroom system that monitors students in different ways.

    The system, which cost just under $5 million, tracks attendance and lateness, but is also able to check the “head-raising rate” of students as well. If you’re not looking up at the teacher and paying attention, the system will recognise that and count it against you.

    According to SCMP, some students have rallied against the system on social media, forcing the university to scrap the tracking of head-raising rates. However, that hasn’t stopped other schools from going ahead with it.

    Recent findings suggest that SCMP noted that the China University of Mining and Technology in Jiangsu tracks the “classroom status” of students. This identified students who checked their phones during class, as well as flagging some as being asleep – even though they had been collecting notes.
